ARIMA vs. ETS

2.1 The data

2.1a read in the data
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  .gaps
  <lgl>
1 FALSE
2.1b plot the data
sales_plot <- liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly US liquor sales",
    x = "Year", y = "Sales (millions of dollars)"
  )

sales_plot
sales_seasonal_plot <- liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal plot of monthly US liquor sales",
    x = "Month", y = "Log Sales"
  )

sales_seasonal_plot

There’s clear trend and seasonal pattern in the series. The series is overall trending upward each year and it also has a strong seasonal component. It has got an annual pattern in which the sales are highest in December and lowest in January. Since the series is trending upward and the seasonal swings do grow with the level of the series, we should use log transformation to stabilize the variance.

2.2 Fit Both Models

2.2a fit ARIMA and ETS models
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()

  Initial states:
     l[0]         b[0]      s[0]      s[-1]        s[-2]       s[-3]      s[-4]
 7.412219 0.0007608238 0.3263441 0.03153301 -0.004849389 -0.03530501 0.02512163
      s[-5]      s[-6]      s[-7]       s[-8]      s[-9]     s[-10]     s[-11]

  sigma^2:  7e-04

      AIC      AICc       BIC 
-489.1517 -487.2272 -424.2608

The ARIMA model is ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1) with a seasonal period of 12, and the ETS model is ETS(A,A,A), an additive Holt-Winters model. The ARIMA model gets one seasonal difference and no regular difference. The ETS model has an additive error component, an additive trend component and an additive seasonality component.

2.2b ljung-box test for residuals in ARIMA model
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()
liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 1+2+2+1)
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .model lb_stat lb_pvalue
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 arima     120.         0

The residuals do somewhat look like white noise, but by observing the ACF we could see that the series can be significantly correlated with some seasonal lags. The Ljung-Box test also shows that the p-value is essentially 0, which is less than 0.05, indicating that the residuals are not white noise.

2.3 The Horse Race

2.3a expanding-window TS-CV
liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))

liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

There will be 216 forecast origins in total. The first forecast origin will be December 2001, and the last forecast origin will be November 2019.

2.3b produce one-month-ahead forecasts and compute accuracy
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) 
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  .model .type  RMSE   MAE
  <chr>  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 arima  Test   81.4  65.7
2 ets    Test   94.4  72.3
3 snaive Test  161.  137.

The first forecast will be January 2002, and the last forecast will be December 2019.

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

The ARIMA model has the lowest RMSE and MAE, indicating that it forecasts most accurately among the three models. The two metrics agree.

2.4 Are the Differences Significant?

ARIMA v. ETS
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$ets
DM = -2.9062, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.004042
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
ARIMA v. SNAIVE
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$snaive
DM = -10.755, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

For the comparison between ARIMA and ETS, the DM statistic is -2.91 with its absolute value larger than 1.96. Thee p-value is 0.004, which is less than 0.05. For the comparison between ARIMA and SNAIVE, the DM statistic is -10.76 with its absolute value larger than 1.96. The p-value is less than 2.2e-16, which is far less than 0.05. Both DM tests’ results indicate that the ARIMA model is making better forecasts and the difference in forecast accuracy between the two models is statistically significant. In other words, the ARIMA model is significantly more accurate than the ETS and SNAIVE models. If I were the liquor store chain, I will use the ARIMA model to forecast the monthly liquor sales in the future.

Forecast Combination

3a. equal weight combination of ARIMA and ETS
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  .model .type  RMSE   MAE
  <chr>  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 arima  Test   81.4  65.7
2 combo  Test   85.2  66.8
3 ets    Test   94.4  72.3
4 snaive Test  161.  137. 
liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
combo Test 85.19 66.77
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

The combination, with larger RMSE and MAE, does not beat the ARIMA model. It does beat ETS that goes into it as well as the seasonal random walk model.

3b. correlation between forecast errors in models
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
[1] 0.8782932

There is a high positive correlation of 0.88 between the forecast errors of the ARIMA and ETS models. This indicates that the two models tend to make similar errors in their forecasts, which can limit the benefits of combining them from the very beginning. Additionally, the DM test says ARIMA is significantly better than ETS. The RMSE in the table also confirms that ETS is performing substantively worse than ARIMA. In this sense, it is reasonable that the equal weight combination does not beat the ARIMA model since the equal weighting will pull the performance of the combination down away from the level of the better model.

VAR vs. BVAR

4.1a read in data
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))
4.1b process data
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

4.1c set up the TS-CV
N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]

We will be producing 120 forecasts for each variable. The date of the first forecast will be 1990 Q1 (shown as 1990-03-01) and the date of the last forecast will be 2019 Q4 (shown as 2019-12-01).

4.2. OLS VARs
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}


rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5130384 0.4598547 2.4927057 0.1956584 0.2084055 0.1988068 0.3902989 0.3610310 
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5693241 0.5268484 2.5212629 0.2277561 0.2069608 0.2153966 0.4973504 0.3789663

The VAR(1) has a smaller RMSE for 7 out of 8 variables, meaning that it forecasts better than VAR(4). Since the VAR(1) is basically a form of VAR(4) when the coefficient for all the latter three lags equals to 0 (an extreme form of the shrinkage we talked about in class), the difference between the two models are the excessive lag parameters. The key is that the redundant parameters in the VAR(4) could bring more in-sample fitting while risking overfitting the model, bringing more noise into the model. Thus, the out-of-sample forecast could perform worse with the estimation errors and noise carried along.

4.3. A BVAR
fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
readRDS("results/var_results.rds") 
# A tibble: 8 × 5
  Variable `VAR(1)` `VAR(4)` `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3` `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05`
  <chr>       <dbl>    <dbl>                   <dbl>                    <dbl>
1 gdp         0.513    0.569                   0.539                    0.567
2 cons        0.460    0.527                   0.486                    0.495
3 inv         2.49     2.52                    2.39                     2.70 
4 emp         0.196    0.228                   0.211                    0.315
5 infl        0.208    0.207                   0.197                    0.330
6 unrate      0.199    0.215                   0.203                    0.216
7 ffr         0.390    0.497                   0.414                    0.358
8 gs10        0.361    0.379                   0.359                    0.362

The BVAR(4) with lamba equals to 0.3 has smaller RMSE for all the variables than OLS VAR(4). This means that with the shrinkage, the BVAR with same number of variables and lags as an OLS VAR can tackle the overfitting problem to some extent. The BVAR(4) with lamba equals to 0.3 has smaller RMSE for 3 out of 8 variables than OLS VAR(1) model. This means that the smaller number of lags included in the VAR(1) can also be helpful to tackle the overfitting problem. When lambda equals to 0.05, our prior becomes much tighter, suggesting that we are more confident in that guess. Thus, the shrinkage becomes heavier with every lag coefficient getting pulled close to its prior mean of zero, which would be close to a simple benchmark mean model. It would not be a fair estimate of how accurately it will forecast in the future. A fair estimate would require testing the chosen model on some new pseudo out-of-sample data and we also need a DM-test to confirm the statistical significance of the difference between the models.

4.3c DM-test
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  e_var4e_bvar
DM = 2.1366, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.03468
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
e_var4 <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_var4[, 6]
e_bvar <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_bvar_03[, 6]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  e_var4e_bvar
DM = 1.7905, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.07592
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Both dm-test results suggest that, for GDP growth and unemployment rate, forecast produced by the BVAR(4) with lambda equals to 0.3 is performing better than the OLS VAR(4) model at either the 5% or 10% level.
This suggests that shrinkage does help to tackle the problem brought by adding parameters. However, at the mean time, there are some uncertainty. Since many of the differences are small and not necessarily statitically significant, reading the rakings in that table should be more cautious.

Factor Model

5.1. the data

md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
[1] 718 122
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
  INDPRO   PAYEMS CPIAUCSL FEDFUNDS 
       5        5        6        2

The “INDPRO” and “PAYEMS” are both transformed into growth rate, the “CPIAUCSL” is transformed into change in the growth rate, the “FEDFUNDS” is transformed into first difference. The “INDPRO” may be a series of its own level trending upward while the “FEDFUNDS” being a series of growth rate with a trend. In this sense, the results would be more informative and easier to interpret after taking logs of the “INDPRO” and first difference of the “FEDFUNDS”.

5.3. Replicate the Horse Race from Class

ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
  RMSE_AR   RMSE_FA 
0.6168431 0.5887272

To estimate the factors once, using the full sample, and then use those in the horse race is cheating because it causes information leakage. The factors are estimated using the information from the full sample, which includes the future information that we are not supposed to know standing at the forecast origin in the TS-CV. This might lead to overly optimistic results and does not reflect the true out-of-sample forecasting performance of the model.

5.4. a direct forecast of inflation
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  series   forecasts RMSE_AR RMSE_FA MAE_AR MAE_FA DM_pvalue
  <chr>        <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 CPIAUCSL       349    2.11    1.89   1.58   1.35  0.000443

The factors improve the forecast of 12-month CPI inflation. It reduces the RMSE by 10.4%. The difference is also statistically significant because the p-value of the DM test is much less than 0.05. This suggests that the factor-augmented model provides a significantly better forecast of inflation than the simple AR model.

Reflection

Across the horse races of models, simple models are hard to beat when the data is limited, especially short relative to the number of parameters. With limited data, every additional estimated parameters adds estimation error and noise to the model. In these scenarios, simple models perform well because of their parsimony in parameters. For example, the VAR(1) outperformed the VAR(4) model. The BVAR(4) with shrinkage outperformed the OLS VAR(4). The factor-augmented model outperformed the simple AR model in forecasting 12-month CPI inflation. However, too simple or too much shrinkage can be harmful, as seen in the failure of SNAIVE model and the BVAR(4) with lambda equals to 0.05, which performed worse than the OLS VAR(4) model.

One idea that appeared repeatedly is that shrinkage, equal-weight combination, and factors all tackle the same problem: instead of estimating many parameters freely, they impose structure (pulling coefficients toward zero, fixing the weights, or compressing 121 series into three factors), trading a little bias for a large reduction in variance. Another recurring idea is that RMSE rankings alone are not enough, and DM tests are needed to judge whether differences in accuracy are statistically meaningful or just noise. Finally, every evaluation had to avoid information leakage by using only data available at each forecast origin, whether in the expanding-window TS-CV or when re-estimating the factors. Overall, good forecasting is about an elegant balance - using the useful information as much as possible without overfitting.
